blocks.content: Closing the Loop on Pattern Introduction
blocks.text: Closing the Loop on Pattern Introduction

blocks.content: We have spent this module talking about what design patterns are, why they exist, and how they help us name recurring shapes in code.
Before we go deep into Creational, Structural, and Behavioral patterns one family at a time, it is worth pausing on a more practical question.
Given a real problem sitting in front of you, how do you actually decide which pattern, if any, applies.
This lesson is a short decision framework for exactly that. Think of it as a compass you carry into the next few modules, not a rulebook.
A pattern is not something you reach for because it is elegant. It is something you reach for because something in your system genuinely varies and needs a name.
That single sentence is the filter behind almost every good pattern decision. Keep it in mind as we go.
1. Why You Need a Decision Framework at All
blocks.text: 1. Why You Need a Decision Framework at All

blocks.content: New pattern learners tend to swing between two extremes.
Either they see patterns everywhere and wrap every class in a Factory and a Strategy, or they see patterns nowhere and write flat procedural code even when a pattern would clearly help.
Both extremes come from the same root cause, which is skipping the diagnostic step and jumping straight to a solution.

blocks.title: The core habit
blocks.content: Always name what is varying before you name which pattern to use. The variation comes first, the pattern comes second.
A decision framework forces you to slow down for thirty seconds and ask a few sharp questions before you touch any pattern name.
Those thirty seconds save hours of unnecessary abstraction later, and they are the entire subject of this lesson.
2. Questions to Ask First
blocks.text: 2. Questions to Ask First

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499322369-131477802.png
blocks.alt: Flow showing the three diagnostic questions narrowing down to a pattern family

blocks.content: Question One: What Is Actually Varying Here
blocks.text: Question One: What Is Actually Varying Here

blocks.content: Every pattern exists to isolate one axis of change from the rest of the system.
Before naming a pattern, name the axis. Is it the type of object being created, the algorithm being run, the structure of a hierarchy, or the way two components talk.
If you cannot describe the variation in one plain sentence, you are not ready to pick a pattern yet.
Question Two: Is This Variation Likely More Than Once
blocks.text: Question Two: Is This Variation Likely More Than Once

blocks.content: A single, permanent choice does not need a pattern. Patterns earn their keep when a decision point will be revisited, extended, or swapped again.
If a piece of logic has changed twice already, or you can already picture a third variant on the roadmap, that is a strong signal.
If it has never changed and probably never will, plain code beats an early abstraction.
Question Three: Does This Need to Be Swappable at Runtime
blocks.text: Question Three: Does This Need to Be Swappable at Runtime

blocks.content: Some variation is fixed at compile time or deployment time. Other variation must flip while the program is running, based on user input, configuration, or state.
Runtime swappability usually points toward object composition, such as Strategy or State, rather than compile time constructs like generics or subclassing.

["Name the axis of variation in one sentence","Check whether it repeats or is a one-off decision","Check whether it must change at runtime or only at build time","Only then look for a pattern that matches the answer"]
items: Name the axis of variation in one sentence
Check whether it repeats or is a one-off decision
Check whether it must change at runtime or only at build time
Only then look for a pattern that matches the answer

blocks.title: A useful gut check
blocks.content: If you can solve the problem with a single well-named function and no new classes, do that first. Patterns should remove complexity, not add ceremony.
3. From Variation to Pattern Family, Visually
blocks.text: 3. From Variation to Pattern Family, Visually

blocks.content: The three questions above collapse into a simple routing decision. Once you know the category of variation, you already know which family of patterns to search inside.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783494283984-292994168.png
blocks.alt: Decision flow from what is varying to Creational, Structural, or Behavioral pattern family

blocks.content: Notice that the diagram never tells you the exact pattern. It only narrows the search from dozens of patterns down to a handful.
That narrowing is most of the work. Picking the exact pattern inside a family is comparatively easy once you know which family to look in.

5. A Worked Decision: Notification Delivery
blocks.text: 5. A Worked Decision: Notification Delivery

blocks.content: The Scenario
blocks.text: The Scenario

blocks.content: Imagine an order system that must notify a customer after checkout. Today it sends an email. Product wants SMS soon, and push notifications after that.
Applying question one, what varies is the delivery channel, not the fact that a notification happens at all.
Applying question two, this has already grown from one channel to a planned three, so it is not a one-off.
Applying question three, the channel could plausibly be chosen per user preference at runtime, which strengthens the case further.
That combination points squarely at the Behavioral family, and specifically at Strategy, since we are swapping an algorithm, in this case a delivery algorithm, behind one interface.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499326561-591983833.png
blocks.alt: Diagram summarizing the notification delivery reasoning chain from varying channel to the Strategy pattern

blocks.content: Notice that the code never mentions the word Strategy. The pattern name is a label we apply after recognizing the shape, not something we type first.

blocks.title: Why not an if/else chain
blocks.text: A single if/else on channel type works fine for two channels. Once push notifications, retries, and per-user preferences join in, the conditional grows tangled. Strategy keeps each channel isolated and testable on its own.

blocks.content: 6. A Worked Decision: Reading Configuration Files
blocks.text: 6. A Worked Decision: Reading Configuration Files

blocks.content: The Scenario
blocks.text: The Scenario

blocks.content: A tool needs to load configuration that might arrive as JSON today, and YAML or environment variables later, depending on deployment.
Question one: what varies is how a compatible configuration object gets built from different raw formats.
Question two: yes, this has already been asked for twice by different teams, so it repeats.
Question three: the exact format is usually known at startup, not mid run, so runtime swapping matters less here than in the notification example.
This combination points to the Creational family, specifically something like Factory Method, since the goal is producing a consistent configuration object from varying construction paths.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499329226-687681526.png
blocks.alt: Diagram summarizing the configuration loading reasoning chain from varying raw format to the Factory Method pattern

blocks.content: The factory hides the branching logic behind one call, and every caller gets back the same shape of object regardless of the original format.
Compare this to the notification example. There the variation lived in ongoing behavior. Here the variation lives in a one time construction step.

blocks.title: Spotting the difference
blocks.content: Creational patterns answer "how do I build this correctly." Behavioral patterns answer "how do I let this act differently." Structural patterns answer "how do I connect or reshape these pieces." Keep those three verbs in mind: build, act, connect.
7. A Short Self-Check Before You Commit
blocks.text: 7. A Short Self-Check Before You Commit

blocks.content: Before writing the first line of a pattern implementation, run through a short checklist.
This takes less than a minute and catches most premature abstraction before it costs you anything.
The Checklist
blocks.text: The Checklist

blocks.content: ["Can I state the varying axis in one plain sentence","Have I seen this variation happen at least twice, or do I have strong evidence it will","Do I know whether the choice needs to change at runtime or only at deploy time","Does the quick reference table point me toward one family, not three","Would a plain function or a simple if statement genuinely be harder to maintain than the pattern"]
items: Can I state the varying axis in one plain sentence
Have I seen this variation happen at least twice, or do I have strong evidence it will
Do I know whether the choice needs to change at runtime or only at deploy time
Does the quick reference table point me toward one family, not three
Would a plain function or a simple if statement genuinely be harder to maintain than the pattern

blocks.content: If you answer yes to most of these, you are picking a pattern for the right reasons.
If you are answering mostly no, it is worth writing the plain version first and revisiting the pattern once the variation actually shows up.
A Note on Refactoring Toward a Pattern
blocks.text: A Note on Refactoring Toward a Pattern

blocks.content: You rarely need to guess a pattern correctly on the first attempt.
A common and healthy workflow is to write the simplest working code, notice the variation repeating a second or third time, and only then refactor toward the matching pattern.

blocks.title: Refactor, do not predict
blocks.content: It is easier and safer to refactor plain code into a pattern once the need is proven than to predict the need up front and guess wrong.
8. Common Mistakes When Picking a Pattern
blocks.text: 8. Common Mistakes When Picking a Pattern

blocks.content: Even with a framework, a few habits derail pattern selection. Watching for them is as useful as the framework itself.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499331273-441181224.png
blocks.alt: Diagram showing three common mistakes all leading to a wrong or premature abstraction

blocks.content: Forcing a Pattern to Fit
blocks.text: Forcing a Pattern to Fit

blocks.content: If you decide you want to use Observer before you understand what varies, you will bend the problem to fit the pattern instead of the other way around.
Confusing Structural Similarity With the Same Problem
blocks.text: Confusing Structural Similarity With the Same Problem

blocks.content: Two problems can look similar on the surface, one object depending on another, while the actual variation differs completely. Always re-run the three questions per problem.
Applying Patterns to Code That Never Changes
blocks.text: Applying Patterns to Code That Never Changes

blocks.content: If a piece of logic has been stable for years and has no realistic path to changing, wrapping it in a pattern only adds indirection.

{"pros":["A framework gives you a repeatable, shared vocabulary for design discussions","Asking the three questions catches over-engineering before it is written","Mapping problems to families narrows a large catalog down to a short list quickly"],"cons":["A framework can be applied too rigidly and treated as a checklist rather than judgment","Some problems genuinely combine two families and will not sort neatly into one row","Junior engineers may quote the framework without understanding the underlying trade-offs"]}
9. How This Framework Connects to the Next Modules
blocks.text: 9. How This Framework Connects to the Next Modules

blocks.content: Every pattern you meet from here forward will map back to one row in the quick reference table above.
When a module introduces Factory Method or Builder, revisit question one, what is varying, and confirm it matches the Creational description of flexible or staged construction.
When a module introduces Adapter or Composite, confirm the variation is really about structure or compatibility, not behavior.
When a module introduces Strategy, Observer, or State, confirm the variation is about behavior changing over time or across contexts.

blocks.title: How to use this while learning
blocks.content: As you read each new pattern, pause and ask whether you would have found it using the three questions and the table on your own. If yes, the pattern will stick. If no, come back to this lesson and see which question you skipped.
This checking habit turns pattern learning from memorizing names into recognizing shapes, which is the actual skill worth keeping long after the names are forgotten.
10. Guidance, Not a Rigid Formula
blocks.text: 10. Guidance, Not a Rigid Formula

blocks.content: One last caution before we move on. Everything in this lesson is a heuristic, not a proof.
Real systems occasionally blend families, or need a pattern that only makes sense once you see the deeper mechanics in its dedicated module.
Treat the three questions and the reference table as a first pass that gets you eighty percent of the way to the right idea, then let the depth of the upcoming modules refine the rest.
Frameworks like this one exist to speed up judgment, not replace it.
With that mindset in place, we are ready to leave the introduction behind.
What Comes Next
blocks.text: What Comes Next

blocks.content: The next module opens with Creational patterns, starting from the simplest object creation problems and building up to more flexible construction strategies.
You will meet Factory Method and Abstract Factory first, then Builder for staged construction, followed by Singleton and Prototype.
After that we move into Structural patterns, where the focus shifts to composing and adapting objects that already exist rather than creating new ones.
Adapter, Decorator, Composite, and Facade all live in that module, each solving a different flavor of the same underlying question, how do existing pieces fit together cleanly.
Finally we close with Behavioral patterns, covering the many ways objects can communicate and vary their responsibilities at runtime.
Strategy, Observer, Command, and State will each map directly back to the Behavioral row in the quick reference table from this lesson.
Keep this lesson bookmarked. You will likely reread it once or twice as each new pattern lands, and it will make more sense each time.
Good luck, and enjoy the deep dive ahead.
